devotions.application:
Isaiah speaks to people who know what a heavy load feels like: “the bar across their shoulders,” a yoke pressed down by an oppressor’s hand. A few lines later, the shoulders change: “the government will be upon His shoulders.” The weight that crushed God’s people is not simply waved away. It is taken up by a child born for us.

Picture a woman who drives her father to dialysis three times a week, keeps his pills sorted, and quietly wonders how long she can hold it all together. Isaiah does not tell her the load is imaginary. He tells her whose shoulders are strong enough. Jesus is the “Wonderful Counselor” for the decisions she cannot see her way through, and the “Prince of Peace” for the hours her mind will not settle. The promise does not finally rest on her strength or ours: “The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this.” God’s own fierce determination carries it through. A light has dawned for people who had stopped looking for one, and He means to keep it shining.
devotions.question: Which weight on your own shoulders have you been treating as yours alone to carry, and what might change if you trusted it to His?
devotions.scriptureBody:
2 The people walking in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of the shadow of death, a light has dawned.
3 You have enlarged the nation and increased its joy. The people rejoice before You as they rejoice at harvest time, as men rejoice in dividing the plunder.
4 For as in the day of Midian You have shattered the yoke of their burden, the bar across their shoulders, and the rod of their oppressor.
5 For every trampling boot of battle and every garment rolled in blood will be burned as fuel for the fire.
6 For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given, and the government will be upon His shoulders. And He will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.
7 Of the increase of His government and peace there will be no end. He will reign on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish and sustain it with justice and righteousness from that time and forevermore. The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this.

14 Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will fulfill the gracious promise that I have spoken to the house of Israel and the house of Judah.
15 In those days and at that time I will cause to sprout for David a righteous Branch, and He will administer justice and righteousness in the land.
16 In those days Judah will be saved, and Jerusalem will dwell securely, and this is the name by which it will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness.
devotions.application:
Jeremiah spoke these words while Babylon's army surrounded Jerusalem and David's royal line looked like a tree cut down to the stump. Into that loss, God promised new growth: a "righteous Branch" who would do what failed kings never managed, setting things right in the land. Christians through the centuries have recognized Jesus in that promise, and God kept His word long after Jeremiah was gone.

That long timeline speaks to our own waiting. Think of a father who has prayed for years for a grown son who rarely calls home. Nothing green is showing above the ground. Yet God says "the days are coming," not that they might. The promise rests on His speaking, not on how the soil looks right now. The name at the end goes further still: "The LORD Our Righteousness." The goodness we keep straining to produce, in our parenting, our work, and our own tired hearts, turns out to be His gift to us. We can wait without holding everything together ourselves, because the One who promised is also the One who makes us right.
devotions.question: Where in your life does the ground look bare right now, and what would it mean to wait there trusting that God's "gracious promise" still stands?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 Of David. To You, O LORD, I lift up my soul;
2 in You, my God, I trust. Do not let me be put to shame; do not let my enemies exult over me.
3 Surely none who wait for You will be put to shame; but those who engage in treachery without cause will be disgraced.
4 Show me Your ways, O LORD; teach me Your paths.
5 Guide me in Your truth and teach me, for You are the God of my salvation; all day long I wait for You.
6 Remember, O LORD, Your compassion and loving devotion, for they are from age to age.
7 Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my rebellious acts; remember me according to Your loving devotion, because of Your goodness, O LORD.
8 Good and upright is the LORD; therefore He shows sinners the way.
9 He guides the humble in what is right and teaches them His way.
10 All the LORD’s ways are loving and faithful to those who keep His covenant and His decrees.
devotions.application:
David prays with two kinds of memory in view. He knows his own record: "the sins of my youth" and "my rebellious acts." Many people carry a moment like that, a cruel thing said to a sibling at nineteen or a friendship dropped without a word. It can surface years later while folding laundry or sitting at a red light. David does not pretend those things never happened. He asks God to look somewhere else: "remember me according to Your loving devotion."

That moves the focus from what we have done to who God is. "Good and upright is the LORD; therefore He shows sinners the way." God guides because He is good, not because our track record has earned it. So David's request is an open hand rather than a polished speech: "Show me Your ways, O LORD." It fits a parent unsure how to reach a grown child, or someone weighing a job across the country. David pairs that asking with waiting, "all day long." Direction often comes slowly, one step at a time, to those humble enough to keep listening.
devotions.question: What old regret do you keep bringing up before God, and what might change if you asked Him to remember His loving devotion instead?

devotions.scriptureBody:
5 In the time of Herod king of Judea there was a priest named Zechariah, who belonged to the priestly division of Abijah, and whose wife Elizabeth was a descendant of Aaron.
6 Both of them were righteous in the sight of God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and decrees of the Lord.
7 But they had no children, because Elizabeth was barren, and they were both well along in years.
8 One day while Zechariah’s division was on duty and he was serving as priest before God,
9 he was chosen by lot, according to the custom of the priesthood, to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense.
10 And at the hour of the incense offering, the whole congregation was praying outside.
11 Just then an angel of the Lord appeared to Zechariah, standing at the right side of the altar of incense.
12 When Zechariah saw him, he was startled and gripped with fear.
13 But the angel said to him, “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, because your prayer has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you are to give him the name John.
14 He will be a joy and delight to you, and many will rejoice at his birth,
15 for he will be great in the sight of the Lord. He shall never take wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb.
16 Many of the sons of Israel he will turn back to the Lord their God.
17 And he will go on before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to their children and the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous—to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.”
devotions.application:
Zechariah and Elizabeth were “righteous in the sight of God,” and still the one thing they longed for never came. Luke sets those two facts side by side with a plain “But” and makes no attempt to explain the gap. They kept showing up anyway. Zechariah went to work with his division, took his turn, and did the job the way it had always been done. That is where God met him: not on a mountaintop, but in the middle of an ordinary duty, at a post assigned to him by drawing lots.

There may be a prayer you prayed so long ago that you no longer say it out loud. It might be for a child, for peace with an estranged brother, or for a body that works the way it used to. The angel’s first words to Zechariah were “Do not be afraid” and “your prayer has been heard.” It was heard, even after years of silence. Faithfulness lived out inside disappointment is not wasted. It is often the very ground God chooses. And the answer reached beyond one household, to a son who would “make ready a people prepared for the Lord.”
devotions.question: What long-held prayer have you quietly stopped praying, and what would it look like to keep showing up faithfully while you wait?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 Then a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse, and a Branch from his roots will bear fruit.
2 The Spirit of the LORD will rest on Him—the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and fear of the LORD.
3 And He will delight in the fear of the LORD. He will not judge by what His eyes see, and He will not decide by what His ears hear,
4 but with righteousness He will judge the poor, and with equity He will decide for the lowly of the earth. He will strike the earth with the rod of His mouth and slay the wicked with the breath of His lips.
5 Righteousness will be the belt around His hips, and faithfulness the sash around His waist.
6 The wolf will live with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the goat; the calf and young lion and fatling will be together, and a little child will lead them.
7 The cow will graze with the bear, their young will lie down together, and the lion will eat straw like the ox.
8 The infant will play by the cobra’s den, and the toddler will reach into the viper’s nest.
9 They will neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain, for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water.
10 On that day the Root of Jesse will stand as a banner for the peoples. The nations will seek Him, and His place of rest will be glorious.
devotions.application:
A stump is what remains after something has been cut down. When Isaiah wrote, Jesse’s family line, the house of King David, looked finished, yet God promised a “shoot” would “spring up” from it. Christians have long seen that Branch fulfilled in Jesus. This hope does not start in a thriving forest; it starts where something was lost.

You may have a stump of your own: a shop you closed and still drive past, a brother you have not called in years, a body that no longer does what it once did. Isaiah does not pretend the cutting never happened; he simply says new life can rise from right there. And the One who rises judges differently than we do. He “will not judge by what His eyes see,” so He is neither dazzled by a polished life nor put off by a messy one. He decides “with equity” for “the lowly of the earth.” The wolf resting beside the lamb pictures where His rule is headed: a world where nothing will “harm” or “destroy.” That day has not fully come, but it is already rooted.
devotions.question: Where in your life does something look like a stump, and what would it mean to watch there for a shoot from God?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 This is the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.
2 As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: “Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way.”
3 “A voice of one calling in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him.’”
4 John the Baptist appeared in the wilderness, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.
5 People went out to him from all of Jerusalem and the countryside of Judea. Confessing their sins, they were baptized by him in the Jordan River.
6 John was clothed in camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist. His food was locusts and wild honey.
7 And he proclaimed: “After me will come One more powerful than I, the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie.
8 I baptize you with water, but He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.”
devotions.application:
Mark calls this "the beginning," and it starts not in a palace or a temple but in the "wilderness," with a man in camel's hair telling people to get ready. The crowds who walked out to the Jordan weren't asked to fix themselves first. They came "confessing their sins," naming what was true, and that honesty cleared the road.

Making "straight paths" can be quite ordinary. It might mean calling the friend you snapped at months ago and admitting plainly that you were wrong. It might mean telling yourself the truth about a habit that has grown larger than you let on. These small clearings don't earn anything; they simply make room.

John never mistakes himself for the point. He is glad to go ahead, "not worthy to stoop down and untie" a sandal strap. That is a freeing place to stand. You don't have to be the answer for the people around you. You can be a voice that points toward the One who comes after, who gives not only water but the Holy Spirit.
devotions.question: What crooked or cluttered place in your life might the Lord be inviting you to name honestly, so there is room for Him to come in?

devotions.scriptureBody:
8 Beloved, do not let this one thing escape your notice: With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day.
9 The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance.
10 But the Day of the Lord will come like a thief. The heavens will disappear with a roar, the elements will be destroyed by fire, and the earth and its works will be laid bare.
11 Since everything will be destroyed in this way, what kind of people ought you to be? You ought to conduct yourselves in holiness and godliness
12 as you anticipate and hasten the coming of the day of God, when the heavens will be destroyed by fire and the elements will melt in the heat.
13 But in keeping with God’s promise, we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells.
14 Therefore, beloved, as you anticipate these things, make every effort to be found at peace—spotless and blameless in His sight.
devotions.application:
Waiting has a way of turning into suspicion. When a prayer goes unanswered for years, for a brother who drifted from faith or a marriage still frayed, it is easy to conclude that God has stalled or forgotten. Peter offers another reading of the delay. The Lord "is not slow in keeping His promise"; He is "patient with you." The time that feels empty may be the very room He is holding open, for that brother and for us, so that no one is lost.

Peter also lets us see where all this is heading. The earth and its works will be "laid bare," and everything we cling to for security will be shown for what it is. That is not meant to frighten but to steady. If the world is moving toward "a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells," then the small choices of an ordinary day carry weight: the apology you finally offer your sister, the honest number on an expense report. To be "found at peace" is less about bracing for the end and more about living now in a way that already belongs to what is coming.
devotions.question: Where has God's patience felt to you like delay, and what would it look like to be "found at peace" while you wait?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 “Behold, I will send My messenger, who will prepare the way before Me. Then the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to His temple—the Messenger of the covenant, in whom you delight—see, He is coming,” says the LORD of Hosts.
2 But who can endure the day of His coming? And who can stand when He appears? For He will be like a refiner’s fire, like a launderer’s soap.
3 And He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver; He will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver. Then they will present offerings to the LORD in righteousness.
4 Then the offerings of Judah and Jerusalem will please the LORD, as in days of old and years gone by.
devotions.application:
We tend to wait for Christmas the way we wait for a guest we hope to impress: tidying the surface and hoping the visit goes smoothly. Malachi describes a different kind of arrival. The Lord His people were seeking would come, yes, but like a “refiner’s fire” and a “launderer’s soap.” He does not come merely to admire the house; He comes to make it clean.

Malachi is honest that this sounds daunting: “who can stand when He appears?” Yet look at the posture of this Refiner. He will “sit as a refiner and purifier of silver.” He is not hurried or careless. A silversmith stays close to the heat, watching closely, because the metal is too valuable to leave unattended. The sharp words you keep replaying after snapping at your sister, or the quiet resentment toward a friend who got what you wanted, are the very places He patiently works. He does not come to destroy you but to draw out what is true and lasting. And the goal is not shame. It is that your life, like those restored offerings, might become something that pleases Him.
devotions.question: Where in your life do you sense the Lord sitting patiently as a refiner, and what might He be gently drawing out of you there?

devotions.scriptureBody:
39 In those days Mary got ready and hurried to a town in the hill country of Judah,
40 where she entered the home of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth.
41 When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the baby leaped in her womb, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit.
42 In a loud voice she exclaimed, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!
43 And why am I so honored, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?
44 For as soon as the sound of your greeting reached my ears, the baby in my womb leaped for joy.
45 Blessed is she who has believed that the Lord’s word to her will be fulfilled.”
devotions.application:
Mary had just received news that hardly anyone in her village was likely to understand, and the first thing she did was hurry to someone who might. Elizabeth was carrying her own improbable child, and before Mary could explain a thing, Elizabeth met her with blessing. There is no rivalry in her voice, though she was older, married to a priest, and might have expected to be the center of the story. She simply asks, “why am I so honored,” and rejoices in what God is doing in someone else.

Faith often needs this kind of company. When a promise is still hidden, like a child not yet born, it helps to sit with a person who can see it with you. Think of a friend who has just told you she is taking in a foster child, half thrilled and half terrified. A glad, wholehearted word from you might be the very thing that steadies her. And if you are the one carrying something fragile, it is no weakness to get up and go looking for an Elizabeth. Mary is called blessed not because everything is finished, but because she trusts that what the Lord said will come true.
devotions.question: Whose quiet, unfinished faith could you bless with a glad word, and where might you go to find someone who will recognize God’s work in you?

devotions.scriptureBody:
4 For everything that was written in the past was written for our instruction, so that through endurance and the encouragement of the Scriptures, we might have hope.
5 Now may the God who gives endurance and encouragement grant you harmony with one another in Christ Jesus,
6 so that with one mind and one voice you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
7 Accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you, in order to bring glory to God.
8 For I tell you that Christ has become a servant of the circumcised on behalf of God’s truth, to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs,
9 so that the Gentiles may glorify God for His mercy. As it is written: “Therefore I will praise You among the Gentiles; I will sing hymns to Your name.”
10 Again, it says: “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people.”
11 And again: “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and extol Him, all you peoples.”
12 And once more, Isaiah says: “The Root of Jesse will appear, One who will arise to rule over the Gentiles; in Him the Gentiles will put their hope.”
13 Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace as you believe in Him, so that you may overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.
devotions.application:
Paul writes to a church split along old lines, Jewish and Gentile believers who ate differently, kept different days, and probably sat in different corners. His answer is not a strategy but a memory: “Accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you.” Before you ever got your act together, Christ made room for you. That welcome becomes the measure for how you make room for others.

Think of the person at church whose way of praying grates on you, or the cousin whose texts you leave unread for days. Harmony here does not mean pretending you agree on everything. It means singing “with one voice” to the same God, even while your accents differ. Paul piles up old promises to show that God always meant to gather unlikely people into one family. And he ends with a prayer rather than a demand: that “the God of hope” would fill you with joy and peace. You do not have to manufacture this welcome by sheer effort. The same Spirit who fills you with hope can widen your heart, one awkward conversation at a time.
devotions.question: Who in your life is hardest to welcome, and what would it look like to make room for them the way Christ made room for you?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 A song of ascents. Out of the depths I cry to You, O LORD!
2 O Lord, hear my voice; let Your ears be attentive to my plea for mercy.
3 If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand?
4 But with You there is forgiveness, so that You may be feared.
5 I wait for the LORD; my soul does wait, and in His word I put my hope.
6 My soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning—more than watchmen wait for the morning.
7 O Israel, put your hope in the LORD, for with the LORD is loving devotion, and with Him is redemption in abundance.
8 And He will redeem Israel from all iniquity.
devotions.application:
“Out of the depths I cry to You,” the psalm begins, and it starts right where we least want prayer to start. Picture a man who has finally told his wife about the credit card debt he hid for two years. He isn’t sure what to say to God, or whether he has any right to say it. The psalmist didn’t tidy himself up first either. He simply asked the Lord to hear.

What made that asking possible is verse 4. If God “kept track of iniquities,” no one could stand. “But with You there is forgiveness.” The Lord is not holding a ledger to use against us, and that mercy moves us to honor Him more, not less. Then comes the waiting, like a watchman on the city wall with his eyes fixed on the east. He can’t hurry the sunrise, but he knows it will come. Your waiting may feel long. Still, the psalm names what is already true: with the Lord is “loving devotion” and “redemption in abundance,” more than enough for whatever brought you low.
devotions.question: What have you been carrying in the depths that you could bring to the Lord, trusting that with Him “there is forgiveness” and redemption in abundance?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 The wilderness and the dry land will be glad; the desert will rejoice and blossom like a rose.
2 It will bloom profusely and rejoice with joy and singing. The glory of Lebanon will be given to it, the splendor of Carmel and Sharon. They will see the glory of the LORD, the splendor of our God.
3 Strengthen the limp hands and steady the feeble knees!
4 Say to those with anxious hearts: “Be strong, do not fear! Behold, your God will come with vengeance. With divine retribution He will come to save you.”
5 Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped.
6 Then the lame will leap like a deer and the mute tongue will shout for joy. For waters will gush forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.
7 The parched ground will become a pool, the thirsty land springs of water. In the haunt where jackals once lay, there will be grass and reeds and papyrus.
8 And there will be a highway called the Way of Holiness. The unclean will not travel it—only those who walk in the Way—and fools will not stray onto it.
9 No lion will be there, and no vicious beast will go up on it. Such will not be found there, but the redeemed will walk upon it.
10 So the redeemed of the LORD will return and enter Zion with singing, crowned with everlasting joy. Gladness and joy will overtake them, and sorrow and sighing will flee.
devotions.application:
Isaiah does not pretend the desert isn't there. He names it plainly: dry land, parched ground, a haunt where jackals lie. Then he promises that God will come into that very place, and water will break out where nothing grew. The vision is not of some other landscape. It is the same one, made new.

Between the blossoms and the highway sits a small, practical command: "Strengthen the limp hands and steady the feeble knees!" Before the full rescue arrives, God's people are told to hold one another up. That might look like sitting beside a friend in a clinic waiting room, saying little, just keeping her company until her name is called. It might mean offering the words Isaiah gives: "Be strong, do not fear!" They are not a scolding. They remind us that God Himself is on the way, and He comes "to save you."

The road also leads somewhere. The redeemed walk it with singing, and "sorrow and sighing will flee." The dry stretch you are crossing, or helping someone else cross, is not where the journey ends.
devotions.question: Whose limp hands or feeble knees has God placed near you, and what would it look like to steady them while you both wait for Him?

devotions.scriptureBody:
4 Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: Rejoice!
5 Let your gentleness be apparent to all. The Lord is near.
6 Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God.
7 And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.
devotions.application:
Paul wrote these words while in custody, not in comfort, and still he repeats himself: "Rejoice!" He is not demanding a cheerful mood on command. The joy he means is "in the Lord," rooted in Someone who stays steady when circumstances do not. Then he gives the reason underneath it all: "The Lord is near."

Picture sitting in a hospital parking lot, engine off, about to walk in with your father to hear his test results. Worry floods in with a dozen what-ifs. Paul does not scold that fear; he gives it somewhere to go. His phrase "in everything" covers the small and the frightening alike: finding a parking spot, the doctor's tone, the words you will need afterward. Name each one to God, and tuck in thanks where you can find it, for the drive there together or the nurse who remembered his name. What comes back may not be the answer you asked for, but a peace that "surpasses all understanding," standing watch over your heart and mind like a guard at a gate. From that quiet center, gentleness toward others can grow.
devotions.question: Which worry are you holding most tightly, and what would it look like to hand it to God alongside one honest word of thanks?

devotions.scriptureBody:
2 Meanwhile John heard in prison about the works of Christ, and he sent his disciples
3 to ask Him, “Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?”
4 Jesus replied, “Go back and report to John what you hear and see:
5 The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor.
6 Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me.”
7 As John’s disciples were leaving, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed swaying in the wind?
8 Otherwise, what did you go out to see? A man dressed in fine clothes? Look, those who wear fine clothing are found in kings’ palaces.
9 What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.
10 This is the one about whom it is written: ‘Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way before You.’
11 Truly I tell you, among those born of women there has risen no one greater than John the Baptist. Yet even the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.
devotions.application:
John had baptized Jesus and heard the voice from heaven, yet in a prison cell his certainty wavered: “Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?” Doubt can arrive like that, after years of faithfulness, when life narrows to four walls, such as a hospital room, a marriage gone quiet, or a job that ended without warning. John did not hide his question. He sent it straight to Jesus.

Jesus did not scold him. He sent back what was happening: the blind seeing, the lame walking, good news reaching the poor. He pointed John to what God was already doing, even if it did not look like the rescue John may have hoped for. Then, as the messengers left, Jesus honored John before the crowd. The man with the hard question was still “more than a prophet.” Your questions do not disqualify you either. You can bring them to Jesus honestly, and you can watch for His quieter works, like a neighbor who shows up with soup or a reconciliation you had given up on. He knows the cell you sit in, and He is not ashamed of the one who asks.
devotions.question: What honest question would you bring to Jesus right now, and where might you already see signs of His work around you?

devotions.scriptureBody:
14 Sing for joy, O Daughter of Zion; shout aloud, O Israel! Be glad and rejoice with all your heart, O Daughter of Jerusalem!
15 The LORD has taken away your punishment; He has turned back your enemy. Israel’s King, the LORD, is among you; no longer will you fear any harm.
16 On that day they will say to Jerusalem: “Do not fear, O Zion; do not let your hands fall limp.
17 The LORD your God is among you; He is mighty to save. He will rejoice over you with gladness; He will quiet you with His love; He will rejoice over you with singing.”
devotions.application:
A parent bending over a crib, humming the same three notes until a crying child settles, is close to the picture Zephaniah gives in verse 17. The LORD “will quiet you with His love.” He does not shout over our noise or demand that we calm ourselves first. He comes near, “among you,” and His love does the quieting.

The order in this passage matters. Before anyone is told to sing, God has already acted: He “has taken away your punishment” and “turned back your enemy.” Joy here is a response, not a performance. And the singing does not go only one direction. We are invited to “shout aloud,” yet God is the One who “will rejoice over you with singing.” Hold onto that when your hands feel heavy, like when you are waiting on test results that will not come. The prophet names that exact weariness: “do not let your hands fall limp.” The remedy offered is not a pep talk but a presence. The Mighty One who saves is also the One who sings over you, and He is not far off.
devotions.question: When your hands feel limp, what might change if you pictured God not frowning at your weariness but quieting you with His love and singing over you?

devotions.scriptureBody:
7 Be patient, then, brothers, until the Lord’s coming. See how the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the soil—how patient he is for the fall and spring rains.
8 You, too, be patient and strengthen your hearts, because the Lord’s coming is near.
9 Do not complain about one another, brothers, so that you will not be judged. Look, the Judge is standing at the door!
10 Brothers, as an example of patience in affliction, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord.
devotions.application:
A farmer cannot hurry the rain. He can plow, plant, and pull weeds, but the “fall and spring rains” come on their own schedule, and the “precious fruit of the soil” ripens slowly beneath them. James holds up that farmer for people who were tired of waiting for the Lord to set things right. Patience here is not passive. It is the steady work of someone who keeps tending the field while trusting what only God can send.

Then James turns, almost abruptly, to the people next to us. Long waiting has a way of souring into irritation with whoever is closest: the brother who still hasn’t paid back the loan, the roommate who leaves every dish in the sink, the spouse who sighs at the same old problem. “Do not complain about one another,” James says, because “the Judge is standing at the door.” Christ is near, and that nearness steadies us. We do not have to settle every grievance ourselves. Like the prophets who kept speaking through hard years, we can “strengthen your hearts,” as James puts it, keep sowing kindness, and leave the harvest in His hands.
devotions.question: Where has a long wait made you short with someone close to you, and what would patient, hopeful waiting look like alongside them?

devotions.scriptureBody:
46 Then Mary said: “My soul magnifies the Lord,
47 and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior!
48 For He has looked with favor on the humble state of His servant. From now on all generations will call me blessed.
49 For the Mighty One has done great things for me. Holy is His name.
50 His mercy extends to those who fear Him, from generation to generation.
51 He has performed mighty deeds with His arm; He has scattered those who are proud in the thoughts of their hearts.
52 He has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble.
53 He has filled the hungry with good things, but has sent the rich away empty.
54 He has helped His servant Israel, remembering to be merciful,
55 as He promised to our fathers, to Abraham and his descendants forever.”
devotions.application:
Mary sings before anything has visibly changed. She is young, engaged but not yet married, pregnant, and about to face neighbors who will count the months. Yet she speaks of what God “has done” as though it were already finished. Her joy does not come from her circumstances improving; it comes from being seen. God “has looked with favor on the humble state of His servant.” The One whose name is holy noticed a girl from a small town no one bragged about.

That same attention reaches into small, unremarkable places now. Think of a nurse’s aide finishing a double shift, unthanked, who stops at the pharmacy for her mother’s prescription. Mary’s song tells her that heaven does not rank people the way a payroll does. God fills “the hungry with good things” and lifts up “the humble,” while pride and power turn out to be thinner than they look. This is not a call to pretend things are fine. It is an invitation to let your soul magnify the Lord, to make Him larger in your sight, right in the middle of what is unfinished, trusting that His mercy runs “from generation to generation,” including yours.
devotions.question: Where in your own humble, unfinished circumstances might God already be looking with favor, and what would it look like to magnify Him there?

devotions.scriptureBody:
8 Now then, you are to tell My servant David that this is what the LORD of Hosts says: I took you from the pasture, from following the flock, to be the ruler over My people Israel.
9 I have been with you wherever you have gone, and I have cut off all your enemies from before you. Now I will make for you a name like that of the greatest in the land.
10 And I will provide a place for My people Israel and will plant them so that they may dwell in a place of their own and be disturbed no more. No longer will the sons of wickedness oppress them as they did at the beginning
11 and have done since the day I appointed judges over My people Israel. I will give you rest from all your enemies. The LORD declares to you that He Himself will establish a house for you.
12 And when your days are fulfilled and you rest with your fathers, I will raise up your descendant after you, who will come from your own body, and I will establish his kingdom.
13 He will build a house for My Name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
14 I will be his Father, and he will be My son. When he does wrong, I will discipline him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men.
15 But My loving devotion will never be removed from him as I removed it from Saul, whom I removed from before you.
16 Your house and kingdom will endure forever before Me, and your throne will be established forever.”
devotions.application:
David had plans to build something grand for God, a house of cedar for the ark. God answers by turning the plan around: “He Himself will establish a house for you.” Before any talk of the future, the Lord reminds David where he began: “from the pasture, from following the flock.” The throne, the victories, and the name all came from God’s hand, not from David’s résumé.

That reversal can loosen a tight grip. A father lying awake over his son’s choices, sure that one more perfectly handled conversation will fix everything, carries a quiet assumption: it all depends on me. Here God looks past David’s lifetime to a descendant whose throne will stand “forever,” a promise Christians see fulfilled in Jesus, born of David’s line. The tenderness of verse 15 stands out too. When this son does wrong, there will be discipline, yet “My loving devotion will never be removed from him.” Failure is real, but it is held within a faithfulness that stays. Whatever you are straining to build, you can set it inside what God has promised to build.
devotions.question: Where are you straining to build something by your own strength, and how might it change things to trust what God has promised to build?

devotions.scriptureBody:
18 This is how the birth of Jesus Christ came about: His mother Mary was pledged in marriage to Joseph, but before they came together, she was found to be with child through the Holy Spirit.
19 Because Joseph her husband was a righteous man and was unwilling to disgrace her publicly, he resolved to divorce her quietly.
20 But after he had pondered these things, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream and said, “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to embrace Mary as your wife, for the One conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.
21 She will give birth to a Son, and you are to give Him the name Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins.”
22 All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had said through the prophet:
23 “Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and they will call Him Immanuel” (which means, “God with us”).
24 When Joseph woke up, he did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him and embraced Mary as his wife.
25 But he had no union with her until she gave birth to a Son. And he gave Him the name Jesus.
devotions.application:
Joseph had a plan, and it was a decent one. His future had just come apart, and instead of lashing out, he looked for the gentlest way through: no public scene, no shame heaped on Mary, only a quiet ending. Then God asked him for something harder than decency. The angel told him “do not be afraid to embrace Mary as your wife.” Joseph was asked to step toward the very situation he had been trying to leave gracefully.

Sometimes our kindest option is still a polite exit: the aging father whose care we manage from a comfortable distance, or the friend whose messy season we have decided is not ours to carry. Joseph’s story does not mock that instinct, but it shows that God sometimes calls us closer than feels safe. Joseph says nothing in this passage. He wakes, does what he was told, and names the child. The prophet’s name for that child holds the reason Joseph could do it: Immanuel, “God with us.” Joseph was not sent into the hard thing alone. Neither are you, wherever your own unexpected turn has left you.
devotions.question: Where are you planning a quiet, polite exit from something hard, and what might it look like to step toward it, trusting that God is with you?

devotions.application:
Bethlehem was the kind of town people passed through on their way to somewhere that mattered. Micah calls it “small among the clans of Judah,” and that is precisely where God chose to begin. The One whose origins reach back “from the days of eternity” would come from a place hardly worth mentioning. God has a long habit of starting in places like that: a cramped apartment with a secondhand tree, a job no one asks about, a prayer life that feels thin.

Micah also says, “He will be our peace when Assyria invades our land.” Not after the invasion, and not instead of it, but when. The peace he describes is less a calm season than a Person, One who stands and shepherds “in the strength of the LORD.” If something is pressing hard against your borders, like test results you are still waiting on or a family strain the holidays only sharpen, this Shepherd does not wait for the threat to pass before He stands among His flock. He is already there, and His greatness reaches even to your corner of the earth.
devotions.question: Where in your life right now do you need Christ to be your peace in the middle of the trouble, rather than only after it ends?
devotions.scriptureBody:
2 But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are small among the clans of Judah, out of you will come forth for Me One to be ruler over Israel—One whose origins are of old, from the days of eternity.
3 Therefore Israel will be abandoned until she who is in labor has given birth; then the rest of His brothers will return to the children of Israel.
4 He will stand and shepherd His flock in the strength of the LORD, in the majestic name of the LORD His God. And they will dwell securely, for then His greatness will extend to the ends of the earth.
5 And He will be our peace when Assyria invades our land and tramples our citadels. We will raise against it seven shepherds, even eight leaders of men.

67 Then his father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied:
68 “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, because He has visited and redeemed His people.
69 He has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David,
70 as He spoke through His holy prophets, those of ages past,
71 salvation from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us,
72 to show mercy to our fathers and to remember His holy covenant,
73 the oath He swore to our father Abraham, to grant us
74 deliverance from hostile hands, that we may serve Him without fear,
75 in holiness and righteousness before Him all the days of our lives.
76 And you, child, will be called a prophet of the Most High; for you will go on before the Lord to prepare the way for Him,
77 to give to His people the knowledge of salvation through the forgiveness of their sins,
78 because of the tender mercy of our God, by which the Dawn will visit us from on high,
79 to shine on those who live in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the path of peace.”
devotions.application:
Zechariah’s first words after months of silence are not about himself. With his newborn son before him, he looks back across centuries, to David, to the prophets, to the oath sworn to Abraham, and sees that God has kept every word. Then he turns to the small child and says, “And you, child,” giving this baby a place in a much larger story. The hope he sings does not float above ordinary life. It lands on feet: God will “guide our feet into the path of peace.”

Picture walking back into the shop or office where last week’s mistake still hangs in the air. Zechariah names what makes such steps possible: “the tender mercy of our God.” Forgiveness is not a distant idea here; it is how God frees His people to “serve Him without fear.” The Dawn he speaks of shines on those “in the shadow of death,” not only on people who already feel bright. Whatever room you are in, that light is coming toward you rather than waiting for you to find it first.
devotions.question: What step are you facing where you need God’s tender mercy to guide your feet toward peace rather than fear?

devotions.scriptureBody:
4 But when the time had fully come, God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law,
5 to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons.
6 And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying out, “Abba, Father!”
7 So you are no longer a slave, but a son; and since you are a son, you are also an heir through God.
devotions.application:
“When the time had fully come, God sent His Son.” In the days before Christmas, life can run on countdowns: flights to catch, gifts to wrap, a table to set for relatives who may or may not get along. Paul’s words slow that clock. God was neither rushed nor late. He sent Jesus “born of a woman,” a baby who needed feeding and holding, so that we could be brought into His family.

Paul’s picture is adoption. A slave works to keep a place in the house; a child simply belongs there. It is easy to carry the slave’s posture into ordinary life: straining for approval at work, keeping score in a marriage, fearing that one more failure will get you sent away. Yet God has placed the Spirit of His Son in your heart, and that Spirit cries “Abba, Father!” Abba is the tender word a small child uses at home. You are “no longer a slave, but a son,” and Paul means every believer, daughters included, sharing the full inheritance. When you feel you must perform for your place, you can rest in the name the Spirit gives you.
devotions.question: Where are you still working like a hired hand to earn a place that God has already given you as His beloved child?

devotions.scriptureBody:
9 This is how God’s love was revealed among us: God sent His one and only Son into the world, so that we might live through Him.
10 And love consists in this: not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.
11 Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.
12 No one has ever seen God; but if we love one another, God remains in us, and His love is perfected in us.
devotions.application:
The days before Christmas can turn love into a performance: the right gift, the full table, the cheerful card to the relative you rarely call. John turns that around. Love did not begin with our effort. It began with God, who “sent His one and only Son into the world, so that we might live through Him.” The manger points ahead to the cross, where Jesus became the “atoning sacrifice for our sins,” taking on Himself what stood between us and God. We were loved first, before we had managed anything at all.

That eases the pressure. Loving others becomes a response to God’s love, not a test we must pass. And John adds something surprising: “No one has ever seen God,” yet when we love one another, His love takes visible shape among us. Think of the neighbor who drives an elderly widow to her appointments without being asked, or the brother who finally calls to mend an old hurt. In small, unglamorous acts like these, the unseen God is quietly made known, and His love is “perfected in us,” brought to its full purpose.
devotions.question: Who near you might catch a glimpse of the unseen God this season through the way you choose to love them?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 Now in those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that a census should be taken of the whole empire.
2 This was the first census to take place while Quirinius was governor of Syria.
3 And everyone went to his own town to register.
4 So Joseph also went up from Nazareth in Galilee to Judea, to the city of David called Bethlehem, since he was from the house and line of David.
5 He went there to register with Mary, who was pledged to him in marriage and was expecting a child.
6 While they were there, the time came for her Child to be born.
7 And she gave birth to her firstborn, a Son. She wrapped Him in swaddling cloths and laid Him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn.
devotions.application:
Luke begins the birth of Jesus with paperwork. A distant emperor signs a decree, a governor carries it out, and a carpenter in Nazareth has to travel to Judea with his pregnant fiancée because a registry demands it. Nothing about the trip was Joseph's idea. Yet that inconvenient order brought him to "the city of David called Bethlehem," exactly where the promised Son of David would be born.

Your own life may be shaped by decisions made far above you: a company restructuring, a landlord who will not renew the lease, a diagnosis that rearranges every plan. Luke does not pretend such things are pleasant. Mary gave birth far from her family, and there was "no room for them in the inn." Still, the Child arrived. She wrapped Him in "swaddling cloths" and laid Him in a manger, a trough meant for animals. God did not wait for tidier conditions before He came. He entered a crowded, improvised, unplanned place, and He is not put off by yours either.
devotions.question: What decision outside your control is shaping your life right now, and where might God already be present in that crowded, unplanned place?

devotions.scriptureBody:
8 And there were shepherds residing in the fields nearby, keeping watch over their flocks by night.
9 Just then an angel of the Lord stood before them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were terrified.
10 But the angel said to them, “Do not be afraid! For behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people:
11 Today in the city of David a Savior has been born to you. He is Christ the Lord!
12 And this will be a sign to you: You will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.”
13 And suddenly there appeared with the angel a great multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying:
14 “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men on whom His favor rests!”
15 When the angels had left them and gone into heaven, the shepherds said to one another, “Let us go to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.”
16 So they hurried off and found Mary and Joseph and the Baby, who was lying in the manger.
17 After they had seen the Child, they spread the message they had received about Him.
18 And all who heard it were amazed at what the shepherds said to them.
19 But Mary treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart.
20 The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, which was just as the angel had told them.
devotions.application:
The first people to hear about the birth of Jesus were working the night shift. They were not in the temple or at a feast; they were out in the fields, doing the same watchful, unglamorous job as always. God’s announcement found them right there, and the angel said it was “for all the people.” That includes you, wherever you are as you read this, even in a hospital waiting room where the celebrations feel far away.

The shepherds were “terrified,” and the first words they heard were “Do not be afraid!” Then came a sign so humble it was almost strange: a baby lying in a manger, a feeding trough for animals. The Savior was found in a setting these working men knew well. Afterward they went back to the same fields, but they “returned, glorifying and praising God.” Their work hadn’t changed; they had. Mary, meanwhile, “treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart.” There is room for both responses, the glad telling and the quiet keeping.
devotions.question: What would it look like for you to return to your usual place, as the shepherds did, carrying what you have heard and seen of Jesus?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
2 He was with God in the beginning.
3 Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made.
4 In Him was life, and that life was the light of men.
5 The Light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it.
6 There came a man who was sent from God. His name was John.
7 He came as a witness to testify about the Light, so that through him everyone might believe.
8 He himself was not the Light, but he came to testify about the Light.
9 The true Light, who gives light to everyone, was coming into the world.
10 He was in the world, and though the world was made through Him, the world did not recognize Him.
11 He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him.
12 But to all who did receive Him, to those who believed in His name, He gave the right to become children of God—
13 children born not of blood, nor of the desire or will of man, but born of God.
14 The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.
devotions.application:
In many homes the manger scene may sit on a shelf a little longer, and John tells the same story from a wider angle. Before there was a stable, before there was anything, there was the Word, and “through Him all things were made.” The One who shaped the stars became a baby who needed feeding, and later a man who grew tired and dusty on the road. He “made His dwelling among us,” in kitchens, fishing boats, and crowded streets.

That changes how an ordinary day looks. A hospital waiting room, a strained phone call with a sister, a job that feels too small to matter: none of these places are too plain for Him. John, sent from God, knew his part was simply to point: “He himself was not the Light.” We are not asked to be the light for our families or to chase away every shadow by our own strength. We can point toward the One who is “full of grace and truth,” and rest in the quiet promise that “the darkness has not overcome it.”
devotions.question: Which ordinary place in your life feels farthest from God, and what might change if you believed the Word had “made His dwelling” right there?

devotions.scriptureBody:
11 For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone.
12 It instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live sensible, upright, and godly lives in the present age,
13 as we await the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.
14 He gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds.
devotions.application:
Paul says the grace of God "has appeared," and with nativity scenes still sitting on many shelves, that word feels close. Yet he does not leave grace in the stable. Grace "instructs us." It is not only a gift handed over once and then boxed up with the ornaments; it is a teacher who stays in the room. That teaching happens in "the present age," right where you are. Think of a relative's pointed remark across the holiday table, and the reply already forming on your tongue. "Sensible, upright, and godly" can sound lofty, but often it looks like a breath, a softer answer, a choice made with Jesus in view.

You are not making those choices alone or without a horizon. You live between two appearings: the Child who came, and the Lord who will come again in glory. He "gave Himself for us," not to hand you a checklist but to make you His own, part of "a people for His own possession." Belonging comes first. Being "zealous for good deeds" grows out of knowing whose you are, the way a child raised in love starts to resemble the home they come from.
devotions.question: Living between Christ's first coming and His promised return, where is grace quietly trying to teach you a different way to respond?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 After Jesus was born in Bethlehem in Judea, during the time of King Herod, Magi from the east arrived in Jerusalem,
2 asking, “Where is the One who has been born King of the Jews? We saw His star in the east and have come to worship Him.”
3 When King Herod heard this, he was disturbed, and all Jerusalem with him.
4 And when he had assembled all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he asked them where the Christ was to be born.
5 “In Bethlehem in Judea,” they replied, “for this is what the prophet has written:
6 ‘But you, Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah, for out of you will come a ruler who will be the shepherd of My people Israel.’”
7 Then Herod called the Magi secretly and learned from them the exact time the star had appeared.
8 And sending them to Bethlehem, he said: “Go and search carefully for the Child, and when you find Him, report to me, so that I too may go and worship Him.”
9 After they had heard the king, they went on their way, and the star they had seen in the east went ahead of them until it stood over the place where the Child was.
10 When they saw the star, they rejoiced with great delight.
11 On coming to the house, they saw the Child with His mother Mary, and they fell down and worshiped Him. Then they opened their treasures and presented Him with gifts of gold and frankincense and myrrh.
12 And having been warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they withdrew to their country by another route.
devotions.application:
The chief priests and scribes had the answer ready. Asked where the Christ would be born, they quoted the prophet without hesitation: “In Bethlehem in Judea.” Bethlehem lay only a few miles away. Yet the only ones who made the trip were strangers who had come from the east. Knowing where Jesus can be found is not the same as going to Him.

It is possible to carry a great deal of faith in your head and still stay put, like the man who can recite every verse on forgiveness while his brother’s number sits untouched in his phone. The Magi show that worship moves. They searched, they knelt, and they opened their treasures, giving costly things freely. Then they went home “by another route.” Meeting the Child changed their path, not just their plans. The short distance between what we know of Jesus and where we actually kneel before Him may matter more than any other. And when the Magi closed that distance, they did not find a burden. They “rejoiced with great delight.”
devotions.question: Where is the gap between what you know about Jesus and where you actually kneel before Him, and what would it take to close it?

devotions.scriptureBody:
25 Now there was a man in Jerusalem named Simeon, who was righteous and devout. He was waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him.
26 The Holy Spirit had revealed to him that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ.
27 Led by the Spirit, he went into the temple courts. And when the parents brought in the child Jesus to do for Him what was customary under the Law,
28 Simeon took Him in his arms and blessed God, saying:
29 “Sovereign Lord, as You have promised, You now dismiss Your servant in peace.
30 For my eyes have seen Your salvation,
31 which You have prepared in the sight of all people,
32 a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel.”
33 The Child’s father and mother were amazed at what was spoken about Him.
34 Then Simeon blessed them and said to His mother Mary: “Behold, this Child is appointed to cause the rise and fall of many in Israel, and to be a sign that will be spoken against,
35 so that the thoughts of many hearts will be revealed—and a sword will pierce your soul as well.”
devotions.application:
Simeon spent years waiting for something he could not schedule. The passage gives no hint that he was famous or busy with great works. He was "righteous and devout," and he kept showing up. Then, on one ordinary visit, "led by the Spirit," he found himself holding the promise in his arms: a baby carried in by a young couple doing what was customary. God's answer arrived looking like someone else's routine errand.

As a year draws to its close, you may be carrying promises that still feel unfinished: a grown child who has drifted, a diagnosis without a cure, a prayer for work that fits. Simeon shows that waiting can be faithful rather than wasted. Yet his blessing is honest too. He tells Mary that a sword will pierce her soul. Peace with God does not promise a painless road. It means knowing whose hands hold the road. Simeon could ask God to "dismiss Your servant in peace" not because everything was resolved, but because he had seen God's salvation and could trust Him with the rest.
devotions.question: What long-held hope are you carrying into the new year, and what would it look like to wait for it the way Simeon waited?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 A prayer of Moses the man of God. Lord, You have been our dwelling place through all generations.
2 Before the mountains were born or You brought forth the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting You are God.
3 You return man to dust, saying, “Return, O sons of mortals.”
4 For in Your sight a thousand years are but a day that passes, or a watch of the night.
5 You sweep them away in their sleep; they are like the new grass of the morning—
6 in the morning it springs up new, but by evening it fades and withers.
7 For we are consumed by Your anger and terrified by Your wrath.
8 You have set our iniquities before You, our secret sins in the light of Your presence.
9 For all our days decline in Your fury; we finish our years with a sigh.
10 The length of our days is seventy years—or eighty if we are strong—yet their pride is but labor and sorrow, for they quickly pass, and we fly away.
11 Who knows the power of Your anger? Your wrath matches the fear You are due.
12 So teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom.
devotions.application:
A calendar with only a few squares left is a fitting place to sit with this prayer of Moses. He does not soften anything. Our lives are like grass that "springs up new" and then "fades and withers." Our years "quickly pass," and even our hidden failures stand "in the light of Your presence." Yet he begins somewhere else entirely: "Lord, You have been our dwelling place through all generations." Before he says a word about how fragile we are, he names our home.

That order matters as you look back over a year. You may be carrying quiet losses: a friendship that cooled, a parent who moves more slowly now, plans that never left the notebook. Moses does not ask you to pretend those are small. He asks God to "teach us to number our days," not to frighten us but so that we "present a heart of wisdom." Counting days honestly can make ordinary ones precious: the phone call you keep postponing, the apology you could offer, the slow walk beside someone you love. The God who was there before the mountains is still the place to live as a new year begins.
devotions.question: As this year closes, which ordinary days ahead might you spend differently if you truly numbered them, trusting God as your dwelling place?

devotions.scriptureBody:
21 Yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope:
22 Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail.
23 They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!
24 “The LORD is my portion,” says my soul, “therefore I will hope in Him.”
25 The LORD is good to those who wait for Him, to the soul who seeks Him.
26 It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD.
devotions.application:
These lines sit in the middle of a book of grief. The writer has just described Jerusalem in ruins and his own soul worn thin, and then he turns: "Yet I call this to mind." Hope here does not simply arrive like a change in the weather. It is something he chooses to remember, the way someone in a long, hard season might reread an old letter from a person who loves them.

As one year closes, it is natural to tally what it held. Perhaps it held a father whose memory is slipping, so that each visit he knows you a little less. The passage does not ask you to pretend that sorrow away. It asks you to set something beside it: the Lord's "loving devotion," mercies that are "new every morning," and a faithfulness that has not run out even when your own strength has. To say "The LORD is my portion" is to say that whatever was lost, He remains yours. And to "wait quietly" is not to give up. It is to trust that His goodness is still on its way to you.
devotions.question: As this year closes, what specific memory of God's faithfulness could you deliberately call to mind and set beside the sorrow you still carry?
